note: "Dumela" works any time of day. rra = sir.
mma = madam. You greet a woman with mma, a man with rra.
Dumela → Dumelang when greeting more than one person.
Literally "how have you risen?" — a morning-flavoured how-are-you.
sentle = well/nicely. Lit. "I have risen well."

eng: I am well — and how are you?
note: The natural reply chain: answer, then bounce the question back with wena (you).
tsw: Ke tsogile sentle, wena o tsogile jang?

note: wena = you (emphatic) — bounces the question back.
O → Le when asking more than one person.
The group answers with re (we).

eng: We are well — and how are you?
note: Answer for the group, then bounce the question back.
tsw: Re tsogile sentle, wena o tsogile jang?

note: Literally "where are you (all)?" — the casual greeting.
teng = present/there. "I am around" = I'm fine.

eng: We are fine — are you all well?
note: Informal reply to Le kae?. Lit. "we are there — are you (all) there?"
tsw: Re teng, a lona le teng?

note: Ke teng = I'm fine, Re teng = we're fine — same teng, different concord.
ke = I, re = we — same thanks, different thanker.

sefane = surname (class 7).

kae = where.

note: The one that DOES join two sentences, usually contrasting ones.
kana works the same way.

note: A … ? makes it a yes/no question; kgotsa offers the choice.

note: seswaa = pounded meat, a Botswana favourite.

note: ka jalo = therefore — draws the conclusion.
